text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London regained some strength after the expected early sharp falls to end mixed with some nearbys returning to the positive territory. March lost $3 to close at $1,690 per tonne, while May ended $8 higher at $1,698 per tonne.

Arabica futures in New York closed mixed with front month May adding 15 points to close at 168.80 cents/lb, while July shed 1.35 cents/lb to close at 155.60 cents/lb. The outer months closed 2.85 cents lower to 3.85 cents higher. Attention was focused on the final day of trading for March. March/May traded as high as 44 over with apparently 21 lots trading at 40 over.

Traders said with the March settling as strong, one has to wonder what is in store for May and July contracts given supplies by the end of the third quarter could be tighter than they are now, weather in Brazil aside. Hence, it is more than likely that supply concerns will resurface in the coming months.

MEXICO - There seems to be general agreement that the 1996/97 (October/September) Mexican coffee crop will be below the 5.37 mn bags produced in 1995/96, but there is no consensus on what the actual size will be. Some traders expect the crop to fall to 3.2 to 3.3 mn 60-kg bags while the Mexican coffee council said that the crop is likely to reach 5.0 mn bags.

Production in 1997/98 is forecast to rise to 5.89 mn bags as flowering is going well and producers are exited about the steep rise in world market prices. Meanwhile, domestic consumption remains slack and some traders said that consumption could be so low that no imports will be needed.
It is estimated that domestic consumption will not be more than 600,000 bags in 1997, down from 800,000 bags last year and the traditional demand of 1 mn bags.

AUSTRIA - After a considerable delay the Austrian authorities finally released their coffee import figures for 1995. The total imported in 1995 reached 1.232 mn bags, 14 per cent less than was imported the previous year and 33 per cent less than the 1.837 mn bags imported in 1993.

The main suppliers of green coffee in 1995 were El Salvador (86,900 vs 99,500 bags), Guatemala (90,800 vs 59,700 bags), Honduras (87,000 vs 64,300 bags), Brazil (113,900 vs 369,900 bags) and Colombia (92,100 vs 144,700 bags). The country exported 228,700 bags of coffee in 1995, 40 per cent less than was exported the previous year.
